readTargets.name: Equivalence relations correspond to partitions
readTargets.statement: If $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on a set $X$, its equivalence classes form a partition of $X$. Conversely, if $\{X_i\}$ is a partition of $X$, then "$x\sim y$ iff $x$ and $y$ lie in the same $X_i$" is an equivalence relation on $X$ whose classes are exactly the $X_i$.
readTargets.idea: From relation to partition: reflexivity puts $x$ in $[x]$, so the classes are nonempty and cover $X$; if $z\in[x]\cap[y]$ then $z\sim x$ and $z\sim y$, and symmetry plus transitivity give $x\sim y$, hence $[x]=[y]$ — two classes are disjoint or equal. From partition to relation: "same block" is clearly reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The two constructions undo each other, so equivalence relations on an $n$-set are counted by the Bell numbers, like partitions.

readTargets.name: First principle of mathematical induction
readTargets.statement:
Let $S(n)$ be a statement about integers $n$, and let $n_0$ be an integer. Suppose that
(a) $S(n_0)$ is true (the **base case**), and
(b) for every integer $k\ge n_0$, if $S(k)$ is true then $S(k+1)$ is true (the **inductive step**).

Then $S(n)$ is true for every integer $n\ge n_0$.
readTargets.idea: If some $n\ge n_0$ made $S(n)$ false, there would be a first such $n$ (this is where well-ordering, 2.6, enters — the two principles are equivalent). It cannot be $n_0$ by (a), and if it were $k+1$ then $S(k)$ would be true and (b) would force $S(k+1)$. The dominoes are the classical picture: (a) tips the first one, and (b) says that each falling domino knocks over the next. Both halves are needed — a valid step with no base case proves nothing, and a base case with a step that only works from some point on leaves a gap.

readTargets.name: Method of repeated squares
readTargets.statement: To compute $a^e \bmod m$, write the exponent in binary, $e=2^{k_1}+2^{k_2}+\cdots+2^{k_t}$. Compute the successive squares $a^{2^0}, a^{2^1}, a^{2^2},\ldots \pmod m$, each the square of the previous one reduced mod $m$, and multiply together (mod $m$) those $a^{2^{k_j}}$ whose bit is $1$. This takes about $2\log_2 e$ multiplications instead of $e-1$, and no number ever exceeds $m^2$. Judson’s example: $271^{321}\equiv 47\pmod{481}$, with $321=2^0+2^6+2^8$.
readTargets.idea: It is the laws of exponents (3.31) in the cyclic group generated by $a$ in $U(m)$ (or in the monoid $\mathbb Z_m$): $a^{2^{i+1}}=(a^{2^i})^2$ and $a^{x+y}=a^xa^y$, together with the fact that reduction mod $m$ respects products. The binary expansion comes from repeated division by $2$ (2.9). This is what makes RSA (Chapter 7) practical: exponents with hundreds of digits need only a few thousand multiplications.

readTargets.name: Truth assignments and truth tables
readTargets.statement:
A **truth assignment** for a set $S$ of sentence letters is a function $v : S \to \{T, F\}$. By recursion on formulas (logic-2.2) it extends uniquely to $\bar v$ on all formulas built from $S$:
$$\bar v(\neg\alpha)=T \iff \bar v(\alpha)=F,\qquad \bar v(\alpha\land\beta)=T \iff \bar v(\alpha)=\bar v(\beta)=T,$$
$$\bar v(\alpha\lor\beta)=F \iff \bar v(\alpha)=\bar v(\beta)=F,\qquad \bar v(\alpha\to\beta)=F \iff \bar v(\alpha)=T,\ \bar v(\beta)=F,$$
and $\bar v(\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta)=T \iff \bar v(\alpha)=\bar v(\beta)$. The value of $\varphi$ depends only on the letters occurring in $\varphi$. A formula with $n$ letters therefore has $2^n$ relevant assignments, and listing them with the values of every subformula gives its **truth table**.
readTargets.idea: Unique readability makes the recursion well defined (logic-2.1, logic-2.2): each node of the parse tree computes its value from its children's values. Changing a letter that does not occur in $\varphi$ changes no node of $\varphi$'s tree, which is why only $2^n$ rows matter.

readTargets.name: Tarski’s definition of satisfaction
readTargets.idea: Truth is defined by recursion on the formula, which is well defined by unique readability (logic-3.1). The quantifier clause cannot be phrased as “$\varphi$ is true”, because the body has a free variable; that is why satisfaction is defined for formulas *with an assignment*, and truth of sentences comes out as a special case. On a finite structure the definition is an algorithm. An $\exists$ needs one witness, and a false $\forall$ needs one counterexample. Read as a game, the Verifier picks witnesses for $\exists$ and the Falsifier picks counterexamples for $\forall$; $\mathfrak A\models\varphi$ exactly when the Verifier has a winning strategy.

readTargets.name: Entry of matrix product equals row times column
readTargets.statement:
Suppose $A$ is $m$-by-$n$ and $B$ is $n$-by-$p$. Then for $1 \le j \le m$ and $1 \le k \le p$,
$$(AB)_{j,k} = A_{j,\cdot}\,B_{\cdot,k},$$
the product of the $1$-by-$n$ matrix formed by row $j$ of $A$ with the $n$-by-$1$ matrix formed by column $k$ of $B$.
readTargets.idea: Multiplying a $1$-by-$n$ matrix by an $n$-by-$1$ matrix gives a $1$-by-$1$ matrix whose single entry is $\sum_r A_{j,r}B_{r,k}$ by 3.41 — and that is the definition of $(AB)_{j,k}$. In $\mathbf R^n$ this number is the dot product of the row and the column: their lengths times the cosine of the angle between them.

readTargets.name: Pigeonhole principle
readTargets.statement: If $n$ objects are placed in $k$ boxes, then some box contains at least $\lceil n/k\rceil$ of them. In particular, if $n>k$ some box contains at least two objects, and if $n > mk$ some box contains more than $m$. The bound is sharp: distributing the objects as evenly as possible puts at most $\lceil n/k\rceil$ in every box.
readTargets.idea: If every box held at most $\lceil n/k\rceil-1$ objects, then, since $\lceil n/k\rceil - 1 < n/k$, the sum rule (1.1) would give fewer than $k\cdot n/k = n$ objects in total. The argument never looks at *how* the objects were placed, which is why the principle powers existence proofs such as Erdős–Szekeres (1.3) and Ramsey's theorem without producing the crowded box.
readTargets.scope: Holds for every placement whatsoever of finitely many objects into finitely many boxes. It is a pure existence statement: it says a crowded box exists, not which one.
